document.title: Reviews and buying research answer different questions
document.angle_statement: Reviews can tell a business what clients thought of their experience; asking newly booked clients what influenced their choice can surface a different kind of evidence, potentially useful when shaping ads and landing pages.
document.audience: Wedding-business owners who have customer reviews but want a better understanding of what influences couples’ decisions.
document.reader_promise: Understand the difference between feedback about an experience and information about the choice to book—and see why a proposed post-booking survey could add useful messaging context without proving what will convert.
document.positioning: WARM thought shift: demonstrate strategic curiosity about buyer choice, not a survey-service launch or a software tutorial.
document.why_now: Editorial relevance, not a dated trend: use the selected conversation to revisit what existing reviews do and do not answer [C1–C3]. Do not attach the discussion to the dossier's editorial week as a meeting date.
document.core_insight: Praise about the experience does not necessarily explain the decision that preceded it. Asking about that decision may add a different kind of information, but its answers and marketing value remain unestablished here [C3].
message_spine: Keep reviews valuable: distinguish the question about the experience from the question about choosing the business [C3].
Introduce asking newly booked clients about buying triggers as the proposed addition, not a replacement for reviews [C2–C3].
Show the proposed path from client-sent survey to shared responses to possible ad and landing-page messaging review [C2].
End with clearer thinking, not a result claim: no adoption, response rate, messaging change or marketing outcome is established [C2–C4].
document.audience_pain: Editorial hypothesis: an owner may have positive feedback yet still feel uncertain about why couples chose the business. Address that uncertainty without claiming it describes all wedding businesses [C5].
narrative: Hook direction: juxtapose feedback about the wedding experience with the unanswered question of why the couple booked. Do not fabricate a customer quotation.
Recognise reviews as useful material, then introduce the narrower distinction in C3.
After reuse clearance, anonymously paraphrase the reported onboarding observation in C1; do not repeat the source's universal language as a verified prevalence claim.
Explain the survey/shared-response idea as a proposal throughout, using C2 rather than a current-feature demonstration.
Describe the intended application to ads and landing pages as a possibility, not an observed improvement.
Close with the exact supplied CTA, subject to verification of its current commercial implication. Do not add another offer or destination.
evidence_boundaries: C1 is a transcript-labelled speaker's reported observation, not independent evidence about industry-wide research habits.
C2 preserves planned status: the survey workflow and shared spreadsheet are proposed, not confirmed as implemented or currently offered.
No client participation, adoption, response rate, messaging change or marketing result is reported. Do not supply example answers that look like collected responses.
C3 is a bounded inference. Reviews may contain decision-related information; do not claim that reviews can never be market research.
C4 establishes agreement with an idea, not implementation, acceptance testing or client demand.
Speaker labels are unverified, sensitivity is unknown and supplied passages are not cleared for public use. Prefer anonymous paraphrase only after clearance.
No meeting date or public recording URL is established. Do not infer either from week admission.
Prior arguments, Knowledge Base examples and exemplar briefs are editorial context only, never proof of current services or results.
External research was disabled; supplied research queries are unanswered questions, not findings.
Use no numerical performance assertions. Production slide numbering is structural direction, not a sourced factual metric.

email.reader_job: Understand why having reviews may still leave the reason for booking unanswered.
email.direction: A reflective founder lesson that develops the distinction before introducing the anonymous proposal. Use no case-study ending or invented survey responses.
outline: Open with two different questions: the experience delivered and the choice made beforehand; frame the distinction as C3.
Acknowledge that a review can contain useful information, including possible choice context.
After clearance, paraphrase the reported onboarding observation in C1 without universal language.
Describe C2's proposed survey, client sending/tagging responsibility and shared response review.
Connect possible findings to ads and landing pages while explicitly stating that answers and results are not established.
End with the exact supplied CTA; confirm a usable DM route for email without inventing a link.

carousel.direction: Introduce the unanswered booking-choice question beside an experience-feedback card. No invented testimonial [C3].

Separate the experience question from the choice question using clearly labelled conceptual cards [C3].
Introduce asking newly booked clients about buying triggers as the proposed addition; show a blank question card, not a response [C2].
Show client sending/tagging and shared spreadsheet review as a proposed conceptual workflow, visibly labelled as such [C2].
Connect shared information to possible ad-copy and landing-page review. Use question marks rather than success checkmarks [C2–C3].
Clarify the limit: a useful research question is not a reported response or a proven marketing improvement [C2–C3].
Close with the exact supplied CTA. Keep it readable and add no service availability, offer terms or alternative invitation [C7].
